title: Tailoring polarization homogeneity in discontinuous-columnar Bi(Fe,Mn)O_3 thin films via dislocation engineering with controlled self-assembly

paper_content.abstract: Defect microstructures, particularly dislocations, are pivotal in determining the functional properties of ferroelectric thin films. While their density is routinely considered, the critical role of their spatial configuration has remained largely unexplored and difficult to control. Here, we develop a controlled self-assembly strategy for dislocations in Bi(Fe,Mn)O3 thin films on Ni-Cr that directly addresses this challenge. By employing a LaNiO3 buffer layer, we template a discontinuous-columnar grain structure and guide the self-assembly of edge dislocations along grain boundaries in a topologically-protected configuration. The resulting ordered microstructure promotes a more uniform strain field and more coherent FeO6 octahedral tilting, significantly enhances polarization homogeneity, leading to a lower domain-switching barrier and a more uniform domain pinning effect. Consequently, the BFMO thin film exhibits dramatically superior aging stability after 60 days at 60 °C, exhibiting far smaller reductions in remanent polarization (~20%) and coercive field (~35%) compared to the BFMO thin film grown directly on Ni-Cr. These findings establish a defect engineering paradigm wherein the deliberate dislocation rearrangement is leveraged to unlock superior ferroelectric performance.
paper_content.introduction:
The functional performance of ferroelectric materials is governed by their microstructure, with strain-polarization coupling being one of the characteristics widely utilized in non-volatile memory applications1,2. Defects, which vary from zero-dimensional point defects to two-dimensional interfaces, are inherent in these materials and significantly influence their functional characteristics. Among these defects, one-dimensional topological defects, such as dislocations, have recently gained attention not merely as defects, but as core elements whose configuration can be engineered to tailor material performance3–5.

Traditionally, dislocations have been viewed as harmful, with most defect engineering strategies merely focused on reducing their density to enhance material properties6,7. However, recent studies have revealed that strategically engineering dislocation configurations can actually improve functionality. This paradigm shift is particularly relevant in ferroelectrics, where the spatial rearrangement of dislocations is as critical as their density. A low density of randomly-distributed dislocations can suppress random strain fluctuations and promote uniform domain ordering. However, this configuration typically results in higher energy requirements for domain switching and thus a higher coercive field (Ec)8–13. In contrast, a high density of random dislocations can facilitate strain transfer and reduce switching barriers through interaction with domain wall motion, but may also generate random strain field that lead to nanoscale polarization vortex, resulting in decreased remnant polarization (Pr) and accelerated aging process14.

The profound impact of lattice control on ferroelectric properties is classically demonstrated by applying strain. In ferroelectrics like BiFeO3 (BFO), strain-induced templates can selectively manipulate FeO6 octahedral rotation modes. A striking manifestation occurs in epitaxially constrained BFO thin films under strong compressive strain, which stabilize a metastable tetragonal-like polymorph exhibiting both an exceptionally large axial ratio (c/a ~1.23) and fundamentally distinct oxygen octahedral rotation patterns compared to the rhombohedral bulk phase. This “super-tetragonal” phase, first predicted theoretically in the mid-2000s, exhibits not only giant polarization but also reconstructed rotation symmetries, demonstrating dual role of strain in modifying both polar and rotational order parameters15. Similarly, in displacement-type ferroelectrics such as BaTiO3 (BTO), the interaction between strain and lattice distortions becomes particularly crucial for optimizing distortion pathways. First-principles calculations reveal that uniaxial c-axis strain promotes cooperative Ti-O displacements that linearly enhance polarization, while multiaxial (abc) strain triggers discontinuous polarization jumps through anomalous oxygen displacements16.

Building on the established foundation of strain engineering, recent advances have identified dislocation engineering as a frontier for controlling ferroelectric properties, shifting the focus from applying uniform global strain to deliberately designing nanoscale dislocation configurations17–19. This innovative approach enables the conversion of dislocation configurations from randomly distributed defects into purposefully crafted functional elements, providing pathway to simultaneously enhance key memory parameters: increasing Pr to broaden memory windows, tuning Ec for efficient switching, and significantly improving aging stability. By leveraging the unique, topologically protected behavior of dislocations, guided dislocation self-assembly provides a pathway to control local octahedral tilting and lattice distortions in ferroelectrics15,16,20,21. Such precise control over local structural distortions represent the central goal of modern defect engineering.

Bismuth ferrite (BiFeO3, BFO) is well-suited for memory applications due to its intrinsic properties, such as high intrinsic Pr exceeding 100 μC/cm2 and low Ec below 100 kV/cm22. However, the integration of BFO into thin-film devices presents significant challenges, primarily due to interfacial mismatch strain, which can induce defects during crystallization23. These defects can markedly impair the ferroelectric properties, leading to issues such as severe leakage current, accelerated aging in polarization, diminished Pr and increased Ec values24. Addressing these issues by defect engineering provides a strategy to concurrently optimize polarization parameters, paving the way for developing more reliable and efficient ferroelectric memory devices.

To address the limitations in ferroelectric performance of BFO thin films, one must reconsider the interactions among defect configurations and ferroelectric polarization. A key focus lies in understanding how the configurations influence ferroelectric polarization. A major challenge lies in the fabrication of BFO thin films with controlled defect configurations that can effectively regulate interactions across various levels, from atomic distortions to domain structures and overall ferroelectric polarization.

Here, we have developed an innovative strategy of dislocation engineering via controlled self-assembly to overcome the limitations of conventional defect density-control approaches in Bi(Fe,Mn)O3 (BFMO) thin films. Unlike previous studies that employed SrTiO3 (STO) substrates to achieve low dislocation densities and improve ferroelectric properties25–27, we selected a face-centered cubic (FCC) Ni-Cr substrate to deliberately introduce lattice and thermal expansion mismatch with the rhombohedral (R3c) BFMO thin film. This mismatch is not a defect but a design feature, serving as a source to generate a high density of dislocations for configuration control. These dislocations provide a unique way of probing dislocation-polarization interaction and the impact on ferroelectric behaviors. Furthermore, the metallic nature of Ni-Cr substrate offers inherent potential as a built-in electrode for future studies on interfacial charge behavior, while its mechanical properties also make it a promising candidate for explorations into flexible ferroelectric electronics. We then incorporated a LaNiO3 (LNO) buffer layer, which reduced BFMO/Ni-Cr lattice mismatch from ~3.8% to ~1.0%. This promoted the formation of a discontinuous-columnar grain structure, which in turn provided fundamental control over the dislocation configuration, guiding the subsequent self-assembly.

The strain energy anisotropy effect of LNO plays a pivotal role in guiding the formation of discontinuous-columnar grains in BFMO, facilitating the self-assembly of topologically-protected dislocations along grain boundaries. This interaction between dislocations and grain boundaries introduces an innovative mechanism for regulating functional properties, enabling the dissipation of strain energy through a more uniform strain field, more coherent FeO6 octahedral tilting, and enhanced macroscopic polarization homogeneity. Consequently, the LNO-buffered BFMO thin film aged for 60 days at 60 °C exhibits robust aging resistance, with only ~20% and ~35% reductions in Pr and Ec, while the LNO-free thin film suffers severe degradation of ~90% and ~80%, respectively. These findings challenge the conventional perspective of defects as purely detrimental, instead presenting a design approach focused on controlling dislocation configurations to optimize ferroelectric properties.
paper_content.results:
In perovskite ferroelectric thin films, where multiple dislocation types typically coexist, edge dislocations are particularly influential due to their distinct mechanistic attributes. The characteristic extra half-plane structure in edge dislocations generates substantial strain gradients, quantified by pronounced shear stress and asymmetry normal stress near the dislocation core28,29. This anisotropic strain field breaks local symmetry and induces polarization gradients, establishing edge dislocations as effective tools to tailor ferroelectric polarization. The resulting strain-polarization coupling further enables deterministic control of dynamic responses to external stimuli, offering valuable opportunities for exploring defect-ferroelectric interactions.

To explore these effects at a fundamental level and provide a basis for their engineering, we established a 2D slice model of BFMO single crystal viewed along [100] direction, allowing us to effectively isolate and examine the intrinsic edge dislocation effects on ferroelectric polarization. The [100] direction is specifically chosen for reasons as follows: (i) the Burgers vector (b‖[100]) lies entirely within the observation plane while the dislocation line (t) aligns with [010], and (ii) it provides optimal strain field decoupling. Besides, the [100] direction enables clear separation between transverse strain (εxx) and longitudinal strain (εyy), respectively around edge dislocations, while also allowing distinct visualization of domain wall strains (primarily εxx). This geometric selectivity permits effective isolation of defect interactions and precise analysis of edge dislocation effects on polarization.

We compare characteristic electric field-dependent interactions between an edge dislocation (marked as black “T” symbol, where the vertical stem of “T” indicates the extra half-plane and the horizontal bar shows the termination line of the dislocation) and a ferroelectric domain wall (where ferroelectric domain is the region with uniform polarization orientation indicated by arrows and domain wall represents boundary between adjacent domains), as shown in Fig. 1a,b. Phase-field simulations reveal the fundamental mechanisms underlying defect-polarization interaction, providing critical insights into their role in modulating ferroelectric properties.

The results demonstrate that when the applied electric field (E) is below the critical pinning strength (E<Ec, where Ec is the coercive field), the strain field generated by the edge dislocation creates a significant energy barrier that strongly pins the domain wall at the dislocation core. This pinning effect primarily stems from the strong coupling between the local strain field induced by the dislocation and change in polarization across the domain wall. As the E value increases beyond the critical value (E>Ec), the domain wall undergoes a dynamic de-pinning process, characterized by local deformation near the dislocation core and eventual release through characteristic structural transformations. Notably, in the defect-free BFMO (Fig. 1a), polarization vortices emerge, only when the E value reaches a critical threshold value. In contrast, in BFMO containing an edge dislocation (Fig. 1b), distinct polarization vortices are readily detectable near the dislocation even in the absence of E. Without defects, the formation of polarization vortices relies entirely on E overcoming the energy barrier of the uniform polarization state. However, with an edge dislocation, the strong localized strain field introduced by an edge dislocation couples significantly with the ferroelectric order parameter, markedly promoting formation of vortex through strain-polarization interactions. More importantly, this localized strain field provides an additional topological protection, enhancing the stability of the formed polarization vortices. This process aligns with classical domain wall pinning process but highlights the unique strain effects from dislocations. These insights not only deepen our understanding of defect-polarization interactions but also establish the foundational principles for the dislocation engineering approaches demonstrated in this work30.

To further explore this mechanism at the atomic scale, DFT calculations were performed (Fig. 1c) to simulate atomic-scale edge dislocation configurations, which directly correlate with the edge dislocation observed in Fig. 1b. Comparing the pristine (c1) and slip-dislocated (c2) BFMO systems, where the latter was constructed by cleaving the BFMO crystal along the (001) plane, the dislocated configuration (c2) mimics the core characteristic of edge dislocation through a relative in-plane shear displacement (marked by ←/→ arrows) across a defined interface (indicated by the black-dashed line). This structure mismatch reflects the extra half-plane characteristic of an edge dislocation, indicated by the black “T” symbol in Fig. 1b, where the black-dashed interface line corresponds to the horizontal bar of the “T” notation. The anti-parallel displacements explicitly represent Burgers vector components of neighboring dislocation cores, introducing a shear-liked distortion at the interface that may influence local polarization. Fig. S2 reveals the corresponding electrostatic potential distributions with the statistical-box normal plots (Fig. 1d) to show the potential fluctuation. The significantly enhanced electrostatic potential fluctuations in the slip-dislocated structure are evidenced by extended box ranges and flattened normal distribution profiles, which fundamentally reflect charge redistribution and built-in electric field modification. Additionally, the differential charge density analysis (Fig. S3) reveals distinct localized charge accumulation around O sites and depletion near Fe cations, demonstrating that these variations originate from the significant electron redistribution primarily from Fe-3d to O-2p orbitals. This charge transfer, driven by FeO6 octahedral tilting [arrows in Fig. 1(c2)], couples with ionic displacement-induced dipole re-alignment to stabilize the observed electronic configuration. The resulting symmetry-breaking shear distortion creates polarization disorder, providing direct evidence for how an edge dislocation fundamentally modulates ferroelectric behavior through local structural and electronic modifications.

The influence of edge dislocations on the domain structure (Fig. 2a,b), ferroelectric polarization (Fig. 2c) and local strain field (Fig. 2d) in BFMO single crystal were investigated using phase-field simulations based on Ginzberg-Landau equations. In the absence of edge dislocations, the saturated polarization (Ps) forms a stable equilibrium configuration with well-defined straight 90° domain walls (Fig. 2a). In contrast, phase-field simulations of an active slip system (Fig. 2b) containing randomly-distributed edge dislocations (Burgers vector |b|=2ai, where i=1, 2, 3) reveal that domain walls become distorted and broadened near dislocation cores, forming kinked, bulged configurations. This results in significantly enhanced fluctuations of local ferroelectric polarization. The corresponding polarization switching dynamics under super-coercive electric field was systematically investigated to elucidate the pinning effects of edge dislocations on domain switching (Fig. 2c). Compared to the pristine one, BFMO containing edge dislocations exhibits reduced remnant polarization (Pr) and increased coercive field (Ec), highlighting the strong pinning imposed by dislocations on domain wall motion. Further analysis of the local strain field (Fig. 2d) shows that dislocations introduce significant elastic distortions that influence domain behavior, causing domain walls to bend along the isoenergy contours of the strain field, where elastic strain energy is minimized. Without dislocations, only minor transverse strain (εxx) variations are observed around the domain walls, while the longitudinal strain (εyy) remains essentially unchanged. The introduction of edge dislocations with specific geometric configurations (Burgers vector b‖[100], dislocation line t‖[010]) generates significant εyy and coupled εxx at the dislocation cores. This complex strain field presents a fundamental challenge for ferroelectric modulation.

As shown in Fig. 2(e), in the absence of dislocations, the εxx observed at domain walls originates from cooperative lattice distortions that accommodate polarization switching between adjacent ferroelectric domains, primarily manifesting as transverse lattice stretching or compression. While, the negligible εyy reflects minimal polarization-induced variation in the out-of-plane lattice parameters. Upon introducing edge dislocations with b‖[100] and t‖[010] in Fig. 2(e2), the characteristic “extra half-plane” disrupts lattice periodicity, generating substantial longitudinal compression or tension at the dislocation core. This strong localized distortion, through Poisson coupling, further induces εxx, creating a three-dimensional strain field with significantly greater intensity than domain wall induced local strains.

These results demonstrate that the configuration of edge dislocations exerts a much stronger localized influence on ferroelectric polarization than domain walls alone, as its associated three-dimensional strain field directly impacts both longitudinal and transverse directions.

Structural mechanisms of BFMO thin films
Building on the principle that ferroelectric polarization is governed by dislocation configuration, we designed a heterostructure (Fig. 3) to actively engineer these arrangements. The introduction of a LaNiO3 (LNO) buffer layer between the BFMO thin film and Ni-Cr substrate fundamentally modifies the interfacial constraints (Fig. 3a,b). In the Au/BFMO/Ni-Cr structure (Fig. 3a), direct contact between BFMO and Ni-Cr results in a severe lattice mismatch (Δa/a₀~3.8%). By contrast, the Au/BFMO/LNO/Ni-Cr (Fig. 3b) reduces this mismatch to Δa/a₀~1.0% through LNO’s intermediate lattice parameter, enabling near-coherent hetero-epitaxial growth through optimized lattice parameter matching. XRD analysis confirms that both BFMO thin films possess phase-pure polycrystalline perovskite structures, consistent with the reference (#PDF01-072-7680, Fig. S4). With the introduction of LNO, the BFMO thin film exhibits significantly enhanced intensity and sharpness of diffraction peaks, particularly (012), (104), and (110), compared to the LNO-free one. This improvement stems from the better lattice matching between LNO and BFMO, which lowers the nucleation energy barrier and promotes hetero-epitaxial growth of BFMO31–33.

To further understand the stress environment, we developed a mechanical model treating BFMO thin film (estimated thickness h≈600 nm) as an Euler-Bernoulli beam on a Winkler foundation (Ni-Cr and LNO/Ni-Cr, estimated thickness H≈50 μm), where the axial force (N) and induced bending moment (M) collectively determine the deflection profile ω(x) (Fig. 3c)34. For simplicity, the structure is treated as one-dimensional and symmetric, with interfacial stress originating from the BFMO-foundation boundary and acting uniformly at BFMO. This symmetric stress distribution induces upward buckling of BFMO. Leveraging the symmetry, we restrict our analysis to the right half-region (x≥0), with the symmetry axis fixed at x=0 and the region of interest spanning xє[0, L]. The deflection profile ω(x) of BFMO thin films on the Winkler foundation is governed by Eq. (1).

EIω'''' (x) + Nω'' (x) + kω = 0 (1)

k = E/H (2)

where E is the Young’s modulus of BFMO, I is the moment of inertia, N characterizes the interfacial stress, and k is the elastic constant of the foundation. For the thin-sheet foundation, k is simplified by Eq. (2). We derive the analytical solution under the boundary condition of an applied moment M at x=L. This model directly correlates lattice matching at the interface with stress relaxation on the macroscopic scale, establishing a multiscale framework for understanding how interfacial constraints can be tailored to engineer defects.

Building upon the mechanical model described in Fig. 3c, we perform a systematic comparison of stress distribution within BFMO thin films (Fig. 3d–f). It reveals that the BFMO grown on LNO/Ni-Cr exhibits a distinct multi-directional load transfer pathway, forming a characteristic “square star-shaped” configuration (Fig. 3e). This contrasts sharply with the uniaxial, striped stress distribution observed in BFMO directly on Ni-Cr (Fig. 3d). This fourfold symmetric stress distribution not only provides clear orientation guidance for engineering defects, but also demonstrates improved strain energy dissipation through modified geometric patterning, mirroring reported stress-relief strategies35–38. Besides, the BFMO on LNO/Ni-Cr exhibits smoother deflection gradient with reduced slope dω/dx (Fig. 3f) across the whole thin film, potentially enabling multi-directional strain delocalization. This behavior, which creates a more favorable environment for controlled dislocation self-assembly, merits further investigation through Geometric Phase Analysis (GPA).

To compare the crystallinity of BFMO thin films grown on Ni-Cr and LNO/Ni-Cr substrates, bright-field (BF) and dark-field (DF) TEM imaging were performed (Fig. 4a–c). Both thin films demonstrate excellent compositional homogeneity across their thicknesses (Fig. S5). The thicknesses of BFMO and LNO layer are approximately 650 nm and 100 nm, respectively. BF-TEM and DF-TEM of BFMO thin film on LNO/Ni-Cr reveal discontinuous-columnar grains (Fig. 4b–c, S6, S7), demonstrating epitaxial registry between BFMO and LNO, which is consistent with previous reports39–41. The vertical growth of discontinuous-columnar grains establishes a longitudinal grain boundary network spanning the film thickness. Local selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) of region (c1) (Fig. 4c) shows superlattice diffraction spots with two sets of Bravais lattices, attributed to FeO6 octahedral tilting, which is a hallmark of the high-symmetry R3c phase in BFO derivatives42,43. HRTEM images (Fig. 4d,e) reveal well-defined lattice fringes with interplanar spacings (e.g., (012), (104), (110), (102¯)) matching well with the reference perovskite structure (PDF#01-072-7680). SAED confirms the crystallographic orientations: [22¯1] for BFMO/Ni-Cr and [010] for BFMO/LNO/Ni-Cr, both consistent with the R3c symmetry.

The IFFT reconstructions (Fig. 4g–i) highlight characteristic edge dislocations, marked by white “T” symbols, where an extra atomic half-plane terminates within the crystal lattice, which is a common feature in perovskite ferroelectrics44. Critically, a stark contrast in their configuration is observed: the BFMO on Ni-Cr exhibits a high density of randomly-distributed dislocations, whereas in BFMO/LNO/Ni-Cr, they are preferentially assembled along a discontinuous-columnar grain boundary marked with the red-dashed line in Fig. 4f. This transition from disorder to order directly correlates with the macroscopic strain state. As evidenced by GPA (Fig. 4j,k), the randomly-distributed dislocations in BFMO/Ni-Cr induce a pronounced spatial variation in εxy and εyy, while the self-assembled dislocations in BFMO/LNO/Ni-Cr give rise to a uniform strain distribution. We attribute this to the templating effect of LNO layer during growth. The LNO promotes near-single-crystal order within individual grains. Under the influence of the anisotropic stress distribution (Fig. 3e), this structure actively guides dislocations to migrate and self-assemble along discontinuous-columnar grain boundaries (Fig. S8), using the grain boundaries as effective sinks for defect isolation.

Electrical properties of BFMO thin films
High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) was employed to map spontaneous polarization vectors via tracking B-site cation displacements (Fig. 5a,d) for BFMO thin films on Ni-Cr and LNO/Ni-Cr. The corresponding atomic brightness contrast directly visualizes spatial variations in polarization amplitude and angle (Fig. 5b,c,e,f). Regions from Fig. 4(a1) and (c1) were specifically selected to investigate the local influence of dislocation configurations on polarization (Fig. S9). In BFMO/Ni-Cr, which contains a high density of randomly-distributed dislocations (Fig. 4g), the polarization vectors exhibit significant spatial disorder (Fig. 5a). This disorder arises from irregular B-site cation displacements relative to the A-site lattice, where localized lattice distortions near edge dislocations disrupt the coherent ionic off-centering, creating competing polarization variants evident as random brightness contrast (Fig. 5b,c). In stark contrast, the BFMO/LNO/Ni-Cr thin film, featuring a microstructure with dislocations self-assembly along discontinuous-columnar grain boundaries (Fig. 4i), exhibits remarkable uniformity in both polarization vector alignment and angular distribution (Fig. 5d–f). This direct correlation between the engineered dislocation configuration and the enhanced polarization homogeneity demonstrates that defect engineering is a key to optimize ferroelectric performance. The reduction of randomly-distributed dislocations and their self-assembly along discontinuous-columnar grain boundaries minimizes the random local strain fluctuations that disrupt long-range polarization ordering.

This defect engineering strategy is fundamentally validated by combining it with DFT calculations (Fig. 1c–d, S3). The calculations confirm that a single edge dislocation induces a localized symmetry-breaking distortion, primarily manifested as FeO6 octahedral tilting and the resultant charge redistribution, which collectively stabilize a disordered polarization configuration. In BFMO/Ni-Cr, the collective effect of a high density of randomly-distributed dislocations creates overlapping disruptive fields, accounting for the severe macroscopic polarization disorder. Therefore, the reduction in randomly-distributed dislocations and their self-assembly achieved in the LNO-buffered BFMO thin film effectively mitigate this collective detrimental impact, directly enabling the observed polarization homogeneity.

To characterize the polarization behavior of the fresh BFMO thin films, we measured P-E loops at their respective breakdown strengths (Fig. 5g). The BFMO thin film on LNO/Ni-Cr exhibits reduced coercive field (Ec) with markedly higher Pr and Pm at room temperature. This indicates a lower domain-switching barrier, which aligns with the reduced pinning from the controlled dislocation configuration (Fig. 4i), in contrast to the strong pinning imposed by the high density of randomly-distributed dislocations in BFMO/Ni-Cr (Fig. 4g). Additionally, it also helps in reducing the leakage current density in BFMO on LNO/Ni-Cr, being one order of magnitude lower than that of the BFMO on Ni-Cr (Fig. S10).

Having established the superior initial ferroelectric properties of the LNO-buffered BFMO thin film, we evaluated the stability under accelerated aging conditions at multiple temperatures (RT, 60, 120, and 180°C) for 60 days (Fig. 5h,i). The performance of the two thin films diverges significantly. The BFMO/Ni-Cr thin film suffered severe ferroelectric degradation and ultimately failed at elevated temperatures, while the BFMO/LNO/Ni-Cr thin film demonstrated remarkably superior aging resistance, maintaining functionality even at 180°C. A notable contrast occurs at 60°C. The BFMO thin film on Ni-Cr suffers a severe ~90% reduction in Pr and ~80% in Ec, whereas the LNO-buffered thin film maintains a stable state with only ~20% and ~35% reductions, respectively. We attribute this dramatic difference to their distinct dislocation configurations (Fig. 4). In BFMO/Ni-Cr, the high density of randomly-distributed dislocations creates heterogeneous and thermally unstable pinning sites that are easily de-pinned, leading to rapid polarization degradation. In contrast, the reduced randomly-distributed dislocations and their self-assembly along discontinuous-columnar grain boundaries in BFMO/LNO/Ni-Cr creates a more uniform and coherent microstructure. This engineered configuration minimizes random local strain fluctuations and establishes a stable pinning environment that is robust against thermal stress, thereby ensuring the observed aging resistance.

In situ piezoelectric force microscope (PFM) was performed to probe the domain stability and switching reversibility (Fig. S11). After partial poling with opposite voltages, the BFMO/LNO/Ni-Cr thin film exhibited robust stability, with the PFM phase and amplitude of the switched domains remaining nearly unchanged for over 40 min. In stark contrast, the PFM signals from BFMO/Ni-Cr showed significant degradation within 30 min, indicating substantial back-switching of the ferroelectric domains. This distinct relaxation behavior is directly linked to their dislocation configurations. The dislocation self-assembly along grain boundaries in BFMO/LNO/Ni-Cr creates a stable energy landscape that effectively pins the domain walls, suppressing back-switching. Conversely, the high density of randomly-distributed dislocations in BFMO/Ni-Cr generates a heterogeneous and unstable pinning environment, which facilitates the depolarization fields that drive domain back-switching.
paper_content.methods:
Mn-doped BiFeO3 (BFMO) thin film preparation
The 3 mol.% Mn-doped BiFeO3 (BFMO) thin film was synthesized via sol-gel method combined with layer-by-layer annealing. This optimal concentration was determined through preliminary experiments to effectively suppress leakage current density while significantly enhancing ferroelectric properties (Fig. S12). High-purity bismuth nitrate (99.99%, Aladdin, with 8 mol.% excess added to compensate for Bi volatilization during annealing), iron nitrate (99.99%, Aladdin), and manganese acetate (99.0%, Aladdin) were stoichiometrically weighed. The solvent system consisted of ethylene glycol (99.8%), acetylacetone (99.6%), and acetic acid (99.5%) in a 1:3:8 volume ratio. Bismuth nitrate was dissolved in the mixture of ethylene glycol and acetate under stirring at 70°C, while iron nitrate was premixed with acetylacetone at room temperature. The iron solution was incorporated into the bismuth solution, followed by addition of manganese acetate. After aging for 48 h, the sol was spin-coated onto 10×10 mm2 Ni-Cr substrate at 4000 rpm for 30 s and dried at 250°C for 180 s. Each layer underwent rapid thermal processing (RTP) immediately after deposition. The RTP steps for each layer were as follows: (i) preheating at 200°C for 60 s, (ii) pyrolysis at 350°C for 600 s, and (iii) annealing at 525°C for 480 s. During the annealing of each layer, the underlying crystallized layers experience a repeated thermal cycle. This process provides necessary driving force for the reorganization and propagation of structural defects, such as dislocations, across the film thickness, originating from the lattice and thermal mismatch at the progressive crystallization interface between successive layers. Both the deposition and annealing cycle were repeated 10 times to achieve the desired thickness.

Fabrication of a LaNiO3 (LNO) buffer layer
The LNO buffer layer was deposited between BFMO and Ni-Cr substrate using lanthanum nitrate (99.999%, Aladdin) and nickel acetate (99.9%, Aladdin). Precursors were homogenized in the mixture of 2-methoxyethanol and acetic acid under rotation at 60°C for 2 h, followed by 24 h aging at room temperature. Spin-coating at 3000 rpm for 30 s and drying at 300°C for 180 s were performed with the following RTP steps: (i) preheating at 200°C for 60 s, (ii) pyrolysis at 350°C for 1500 s, and (iii) annealing at 650°C for 480 s. Both the deposition and heat treatment cycle were repeated 3 times.

Structure characterization
The crystal structures were characterized by using X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.5406 Å) (6°/min, Bruker D8 Discover, Germany). The microstructure of the samples was observed by a transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI Talos F200X, USA). High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images were taken by a condenser spherical aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope (STEM, Thermo Spectra 200, USA).

Electrical measurements
The response of domains to electric field after a certain relaxation time was studied using a piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM, Bruker Dimension Edge, Germany) with the writing voltage of ±10 V. For the electrical measurements, Au top electrodes were sputtered onto the top surface with a shadow mask (~1 mm in diameter) to obtain the Au/BFMO/Ni-Cr and Au/BFMO/LNO/Ni-Cr structures. The polarization-electric field (P-E) loops and leakage current density were derived from the ferroelectric measurement system (Radiant RTI-Multiferroic, USA). For comparing the polarization stability, the BFMO thin films were first characterized at RT as the fresh reference, then aged at RT for 60 days, and the corresponding P-E loops were tested. Furthermore, P-E loops were also measured at elevated temperatures (e.g., 60, 120 and 180°C) to further evaluate their stability.

Phase-field simulations of the evolution of polarization behaviors
In the phase-field simulations, the ferroelectric polarization was simulated by solving the time-dependent (Ginzburg-Landau) (TDGL) equation for the temporal evolution of the polarization vector field. More details can be found in the Supplementary Information.

DFT simulations
All calculations were carried out using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). We employed the projector augmented wave (PAW) method to simulate the electronic behavior of BFMO, with the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) and the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional describing electron exchange-correlation (XC) interactions depending on the calculation type. More details can be found in the Supplementary Information.

Modeling BFMO as Euler-Bernoulli beam on a winkler foundation (Ni-Cr or LNO/Ni-Cr)
The mechanical behavior of BFMO was modeled as an Euler-Bernoulli beam resting on a Winkler foundation (Ni-Cr and LNO/Ni-Cr substrates). The governing differential equation was numerically solved using a custom-developed PYTHON-based framework. More details can be found in the Supplementary Information.

Calculation of polarization vector
To analyze the positions and shapes of atomic columns in STEM images, we used ATOMAP, a free and open-source software tool based on 2D elliptical Gaussian fitting. The method involves iteratively fitting the most intense atomic columns, subtracting them from the image, and then extracting the positions of the remaining atoms. More details can be found in the Supplementary Information.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript describes an interesting approach to improving the ferroelectric properties of Bi(Fe,Mn)O₃ (BFMO) films grown on Ni-Cr substrates by employing a LaNiO₃ (LNO) buffer layer. The LNO buffer layer is applied for strain engineering to reduce the dislocation density near the BFMO/Ni-Cr interface (reduced-dislocation self-assembly strategy), thereby mitigating degradation of the electrical properties.
Overall, the work is promising and may be acceptable after addressing the following points:
Comments
1. One important challenge for BiFeO3 (BFO) and related compounds in electronic device applications, including memory devices, is the issue of large leakage current (as described in line. 101). It would strengthen the manuscript if the authors could clarify whether the proposed “reduced-dislocation self-assembly strategy” also helps in reducing leakage current.
2. Previous studies have reported that epitaxially grown BFO on SrTiO3 (STO), with lower defect density at the interface, can exhibit improved Pr and better electrical properties. Since such results are not cited here, it would be helpful for the authors to include relevant references and also to explain their motivation for employing the Ni-Cr substrate, which is less commonly used in Si-based electronic devices.
3. Because the electrical properties of BFO, particularly leakage current, are sensitive to Mn doping concentration, it would be helpful if the authors could explain why 3 mol% Mn doping was chosen.
4. The phrase “industry-standard 60 °C after 60-day aging” might be somewhat misleading. Typically, device reliability tests are carried out at higher temperatures (e.g., 150–200 °C), considering an activation energy of about 1 eV. A clarification would improve the accuracy of this description.
5. In Figures 5a–f, it is a little difficult to identify which regions (e.g., BFMO/Ni-Cr boundaries) are shown. Revising the figure captions for clarity would make the results easier to follow.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript tries to deliver a new concept on self-assembly dislocation and strain field control to tune properties of BFMO films. Although the authors carried out comprehensive studies on the dislocation effects on strains and ferroelectric properties, I do not think this manuscript provides sufficient novelty that readers of Nature Communicaions expect. In addition, some of the statements are rather speculative. The detailed comments are as follows.
I am convinced that the manuscript presents the consistency that the BFMO/LNO/Ni-Cr film is less dislocation density than the BFMO/Ni-Cr film and demonstrates the consequent stress uniformity and improvement of ferroelectric properties. However, I do not see how the authors engineered and leveraged the dislocations to control the strain field and improve the properties besides reducing the dislocations. Although the authors bring up "reduced dislocation self-assembly mediated strain engineering", the conclusion appears to be that a film with lower dislocation density (Fig. 4g and h) is better (Fig. 2c, Fig. 5g, h, and i), which is not a new concept. People have already developed high quality BFO films with lower coercive field and higher polarization (which is not easy to compare due to the orientation difference) even with chemical solution method [10.1002/smll.201903663].
Also, the dislocation self-assembly at grain boundaries is not fully convincing based just on Fig. h and f. To prove the self-assembly, the authors need more data for statistical analysis for any scientific publication.
I am not fully convinced with the lattice matching mechanism for the dislocation reduction for those specific polycrystalline films. Firstly, I do not see the “discontinuous columnar grains” from Fig. 4b and c. To me they look more like granular microstructure. In case of granular grains, the lattice mismatch discussion that the author mention is invalid since the grains at the BFMO/LNO interface are only influenced. Next, even if they are columnar growth, the effects on the dislocation density at grains inside the film are questionable. The lattice mismatch induces misfit dislocations at the interface but does not necessarily produce them in the bulk.
I am concerned with the dislocation effects on the aging and degradation effects (by the way, that experimentation is not for retention study). The films have neither same interface nor crystallinity, which may also affect the degradation after aging. The authors reason the dislocation contribution based on the Ec drop after aging, but it is invalid evidence because the P-E loops after aging (especially for 60 C) do not show proper ferroelectricity anymore. The statement “This distinct aging behavior directly correlates with dislocation configurations” is speculative.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Overall Response to the Editor and Reviewers
We would like to express our sincere appreciation to all the reviewers for dedicating their time and efforts to evaluating our work and for providing valuable feedback. We have thoroughly addressed all the comments raised and made adequate revisions accordingly. In the following section, we provide point-by-point responses to each comment, detailing the changes made in response to the suggestions/comments from the reviewers. Additionally, all modifications in the revised manuscript are highlighted in red for easy reference.
Reviewer #1:
General Comment: This manuscript describes an interesting approach to improving the ferroelectric properties of Bi(Fe,Mn)O (BFMO) films grown on Ni-Cr substrates by employing a LaNiO (LNO) buffer layer. The LNO buffer layer is applied for strain engineering to reduce the dislocation density near the BFMO/Ni-Cr interface (reduced-dislocation self-assembly strategy), thereby mitigating degradation of the electrical properties. Overall, the work is promising and may be acceptable after addressing the following points:
Overall response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer for their highly positive evaluation of our manuscript, especially the remark: ''Overall, the work is promising and may be acceptable after addressing the following points.''. In the following, we have carefully addressed all of reviewer's comments.
Comment 1: One important challenge for BiFeO (BFO) and related compounds in electronic device applications, including memory devices, is the issue of large leakage current (as described in line. 101). It would strengthen the manuscript if the authors could clarify whether the proposed ''reduced-dislocation self-assembly strategy'' also helps in reducing leakage current.
Response: Thanks to the reviewer for the valuable suggestions. We fully agree that high leakage current is a critical issue in BiFeO (BFO)-based electronic devices [Adv. Mater. 23, 669–672 (2011) and Adv. Funct. Mater. 32, 2112944 (2022)]1,2.
In response to the reviewer's comment, we have conducted additional electrical measurements to compare the leakage current between BFMO thin films with high-dislocation (without self-assembly) and the one with reduced-dislocation self-assembly. The leakage current density was measured as a function of the applied electric field to obtain I-E curves for BFMO thin films on Ni-Cr and LNO/Ni-Cr, as shown in Fig. R1 (Revised Supplementary Materials marked Fig. S10). It is interesting to note that the leakage current density of BFMO thin film on LNO/Ni-Cr is nearly one order of magnitude lower than the one on Ni-Cr under the same electric field of 600 kV/cm. The results confirm that the BFMO thin film on LNO/Ni-Cr with reduced-dislocation self-assembly maintains a significantly lower leakage current density. The results clearly indicate that our ''reduced-dislocation self-assembly strategy'' contributes to a notable reduction in leakage current density. On one hand, the strategy significantly reduces the dislocation density, thereby diminishing the number of defects that can serve as leakage current pathways [Nat. Commun. 11, 1762 (2020) and Nat. Commun. 15, 479 (2024)]3,4. More critically, the self-assembly process drives the dislocations to transition from a chaotic, random distribution into a highly ordered, isolated, and periodic arrangement. This ordered structure effectively disrupts the continuous percolation network that readily forms between randomly-distributed dislocations. Consequently, even if charge carriers enter a specific dislocation line, they cannot find a complete conductive path spanning the entire thin film, leading to a significant suppression of leakage current. In other words, self-assembly not only reduces the number of leakage paths but also prevents the formation of an "interconnected network" by reorganizing the pathway, thereby effectively blocking leakage current.
Fig. R1 (Revised Supplementary Materials Fig. S10) Leakage current density versus applied electric field (I-E) curves of BFMO thin films on Ni-Cr and LNO/Ni-Cr.
Following the reviewer's suggestion, the I-E curves have been added into the revised Supplementary Materials marked Fig. S10 considering the limited space availability. Additionally, we have added discussions, reads as: ''Additionally, the reduced-dislocation self-assembly strategy also helps in reducing the leakage current density in BFMO on LNO/Ni-Cr, being one order of magnitude lower than its counterpart on Ni-Cr substrate (Fig. S10).''.
Comment 2: Previous studies have reported that epitaxially grown BFO on SrTiO (STO) substrates, with lower defect density at the interface, can exhibit improved P and better electrical properties. Since such results are not cited here, it would be helpful for the authors to include relevant references and also to explain their motivation for employing the Ni-Cr substrate, which is less commonly used in Si-based electronic devices.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this critical point, which correctly identifies an oversight in our literature citations and the important issue of substrate selection. We will update the references and explain the motivation for our choice of Ni-Cr substrate.
(1) About references and discussions regarding high-quality BFO on SrTiO (STO) substrates
We fully agree with the reviewer's suggestion. The work on growing high-quality BFO thin films epitaxially on STO substrates is indeed foundational research that reveals the intrinsic ferroelectric properties of BFO and is considered a classic in the field of ferroelectrics. These studies leveraged the excellent lattice matching between STO and BFO along with high-quality epitaxial growth to reduce interface defect density, resulting in BFO thin films with nearly perfect crystal structure and high remanent polarization (P), among other excellent electrical properties [Science 299, 1719–1722 (2003) and Appl. Phys. Lett. 90, 212902 (2007)]5,6. These related works have established a foundation for subsequent research on BFO-based thin films.
Following the reviewer's suggestion, we have added the sentence ''Unlike previous studies that employed SrTiO (STO) substrates to achieve low dislocation densities and improve ferroelectric properties25–27, we selected a face-centered cubic (FCC) Ni-Cr substrate to deliberately introduce lattice and thermal expansion mismatch with the rhombohedral (R3c) BFMO film. This mismatch is not a defect but a design feature, enabling strain engineering and generating a relatively high density of dislocations. These dislocations provide a unique way of probing dislocation-polarization interactions and strain-mediated ferroelectric behaviors. Furthermore, the metallic nature of Ni-Cr substrate offers inherent potential as a built-in electrode for future studies on interfacial charge behavior, while its mechanical properties also make it a promising candidate for explorations into flexible ferroelectric electronics.'' into the Part of Introduction of the revised manuscript to highlight the classical approach of using STO for high-quality epitaxial growth and enhanced electrical performance, and then to underscore our innovative strategy of utilizing Ni-Cr to pioneer a strain and defect engineering pathway.
(2) About the motivation regarding the choice of Ni-Cr substrate
The reviewer's concern regarding the relatively limited application of Ni-Cr substrates in Si-based technology makes really good sense. However, our choice of Ni-Cr substrate is driven by a specific scientific motivation that differs from conventional approaches, which also represents one of the key innovations of this study:
I. It allows us to introduce a specific strain state and a high density of defects. There exists a significant lattice mismatch and difference in thermal expansion coefficients between the Ni-Cr substrate with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure and BFO thin film with rhombohedral (R3c) structure. We intentionally leverage this substantial mismatch to introduce a relatively high density of dislocations and strain fields into the BFO thin film. As demonstrated in our study, this distinctive microstructure is not an indicator of "poor quality". Instead, it serves as an essential prerequisite for controlling dislocation density, enabling dislocation reconfiguration, and consequently investigating the physical mechanisms of interaction between dislocations and ferroelectric polarization. Our objective is to explore the influence of defect engineering on ferroelectric polarization, rather than merely pursuing low defect density.
II. It enables the possibility for subsequent device integration. Although Ni-Cr is not compatible with Si, it can serve as a bottom electrode directly for devices given its nature as a metallic alloy substrate. This allows us to construct a simple metal/ferroelectric prototype device for studying physical processes such as charge injection and interfacial transport, a functionality not directly attainable using insulating substrates like STO.
III. It provides a way to explore potential pathways for BFO-based applications in flexible electronics. Ni-Cr offers favorable mechanical strength and flexibility. Compared with rigid substrates (such as STO), integrating functional oxide thin films on flexible Ni-Cr represents an emerging research direction in the field of flexible electronics. Our work provides a foundational technical exploration in this regard. In future studies, we will further investigate the mechanical properties of Ni-Cr (such as elastic modulus and yield strength) and their influence on the microstructure, ferroelectric domain switching, and the stability of the piezoelectric response of BFO thin film under repeated bending deformation. This ongoing work aims to clarify the failure mechanisms of thin films on flexible substrates under mechanical stress and to establish a foundation for developing flexible ferroelectric devices with superior performance and exceptional reliability.
In summary, the choice of Ni-Cr substrate represents a non-conventional design strategy. The core concept is to "turn a drawback into an advantage" by leveraging the significant lattice mismatch to deliberately introduce defects and strain, thereby enabling the exploration of novel physical phenomena that cannot be observed in single crystals or epitaxial thin films without defect (or with low defect density).
We have included this explanation regarding the motivation for substrate selection in the Introduction of the revised manuscript, reads as: ''Here, we have developed an innovative strategy termed "reduced-dislocation self-assembly mediated strain engineering" to overcome the limitations of conventional defect-control approaches in Bi(Fe,Mn)O (BFMO) thin films. Unlike previous studies that employed SrTiO (STO) substrates to achieve low dislocation densities and improve ferroelectric properties25–27, we selected a face-centered cubic (FCC) Ni-Cr substrate to deliberately introduce lattice and thermal expansion mismatch with the rhombohedral BFMO film. This mismatch is not a defect but a design feature, enabling strain engineering and generating a relatively high density of dislocations. These dislocations provide a unique way of probing dislocation-polarization interactions and strain-mediated ferroelectric behaviors. Furthermore, the metallic nature of Ni-Cr substrate offers inherent potential as a built-in electrode for future studies on interfacial charge behavior, while its mechanical properties also make it a promising candidate for explorations into flexible ferroelectric electronics.''. We hope this content can effectively addresses reviewer's concern and better highlights the novelty and contribution of our work. Once again, we sincerely thank the reviewer for helping improve the quality and clarity of our paper.
Comment 3: Because the electrical properties of BFO, particularly leakage current, are sensitive to Mn doping concentration, it would be helpful if the authors could explain why 3 mol. % Mn doping was chosen.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the need to provide justification for choosing 3 mol. % Mn doping. As the reviewer highlighted, the electrical properties of BFO, particularly leakage current, are sensitive to Mn doping concentration.
We introduced a certain amount of Mn primarily to effectively address the inherent high leakage current issue in the sol-gel derived BFO thin films, which is a fundamental requirement and basis for obtaining measurable and highly reliable ferroelectric performance.
Our experimental results identified 3 mol. % as the optimal Mn doping concentration. In preliminary tests across rigid (Pt/Ti/SiO₂/Si) and flexible (LNO/Ni-Cr) substrates, 3 mol. % Mn effectively reduced leakage current to a level that allows reliable ferroelectric measurement in Figs. R2 a,b. This concentration also produced a significant enhancement in ferroelectric properties, as seen in the modulated remanent polarization (P) and coercive field (E ) in Figs. R2 c,d. This optimal performance at 3 mol.% is attributed to the balanced role of Mn ions, which can effectively compensate for charge-compensating oxygen vacancies that cause leakage, without introducing a high density of new point defects that would act as strong pinning centers and hinder domain switching.
Fig. R2 (Revised Supplementary Materials Fig. S12) Electrical performance measurements of BFMO thin films with Mn doping contents of 1, 3, and 5 mol. %, respectively. a,b Leakage current density versus applied electric field (I-E) curves of BFMO on rigid Pt/Ti/SiO /Si and flexible LNO/Ni-Cr, respectively, c,d P-E loops of BFMO on rigid Pt/Ti/SiO /Si and flexible LNO/Ni-Cr at 10 kHz, respectively.
Following the reviewer's suggestion, Fig. R2 has been added into the revised Supplementary Materials marked Fig. S12 considering the limited space availability. Additionally, we have added discussions, reads as: ''This optimal concentration was determined through preliminary experiments to effectively suppress leakage current while significantly enhancing ferroelectric properties (Fig. S12).'' into the Part of ''Mn-doped BiFeO (BFMO) Thin Film Preparation'' in the Methods of the revised manuscript.
Comment 4: The phrase ''industry-standard 60 °C after 60-day aging'' might be somewhat misleading. Typically, device reliability tests are carried out at higher temperatures (e.g., 150–200 °C), considering an activation energy of about 1 eV. A clarification would improve the accuracy of this description.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this highly professional comment. This is absolutely correct, given the activation energy of ~1 eV, industry-standard reliability tests are indeed typically conducted at higher temperatures (e.g., 150–200 °C) to accelerate the aging process. We have carefully addressed this inaccuracy in the revised manuscript and sincerely apologize for this oversight.
Fig. R3 (Revised Manuscript Fig. 5 h,i) P-E loops of BFMO thin films measured at 10 kHz before/after aging (@RT, 60, 120, and 180 °C). a On Ni-Cr, b on LNO/Ni-Cr. It demonstrates superior aging resistance of the LNO-buffered sample.
In the study, we have conducted aging tests on BFMO thin films deposited on both Ni-Cr and LNO/Ni-Cr substrates at multiple temperatures (RT, 60, 120, and 180 °C) at 10 kHz, as shown in Fig. R3. It reveals that at temperatures exceeding 60 °C, the BFMO thin film on Ni-Cr suffered from severe degradation in ferroelectricity, ultimately leading to sample failure. In contrast, the film on LNO/Ni-Cr demonstrated remarkably superior aging resistance, maintaining functional performance even at 180 °C.
While the contrast in aging resistance is most pronounced at elevated temperatures (120 and 180 °C), in the original manuscript, we only selected RT and 60 °C as they provide the most instructive basis for comparison. At RT, both thin films retain functionally measurable and directly comparable ferroelectric properties, thereby enabling a quantitatively rigorous and scientifically equitable evaluation. It turns out that RT condition represents a "relatively moderate aging state" where a valid comparative analysis between the two types remains possible. This is the reason why we selectively presented only RT and 60 °C results in the original manuscript. This striking contrast provides meaningful evidence for our core argument that the BFMO thin films grown on LNO/Ni-Cr, which are characterized by reduced-dislocation self-assembly, exhibit significantly superior aging resistance at elevated temperatures.
In response to the reviewer's suggestion, we have corrected the inaccurate statements and systematically reorganized all the aging data from RT to 180 °C. Accordingly, we have replaced the original Figs. 5 h,i with Figs. R3 a,b. The discussions, reads as: ''Having established the superior initial ferroelectric properties of the LNO-buffered BFMO thin film, we further evaluated the stability under accelerated aging conditions. Aging tests are conducted for both BFMO thin films at multiple temperatures (RT, 60, 120, and 180 °C) for 60 days (60 d) at 10 kHz, as illustrated in Figs. 5 h,i. It reveals that at temperatures exceeding RT, the BFMO thin film on Ni-Cr suffered from severe degradation in ferroelectricity, ultimately leading to sample failure. In contrast, the film on LNO/Ni-Cr demonstrated remarkably superior aging resistance, maintaining functional performance even at 180 °C. Notably, their performance diverges significantly at 60 °C: the film on Ni-Cr suffers a severe ~90% reduction in P and ~80% reduction in E , compared to a more stable state with ~20% reduction in P and ~35% reduction in E for the LNO-buffered film. We attribute this to their microstructure (Fig. 4) with distinct dislocation configurations. The former's high-density, randomly-distributed dislocations create heterogeneous pinning sites that are susceptible to thermal de-pinning. The latter's stability arises from a uniform pinning effect generated by dislocation self-assembly and a discontinuous-columnar grain structure, which suppresses defect migration.'' has been added in the revised manuscript. We thank the reviewer once again for the valuable comment, which has greatly enhanced the accuracy and completeness of our manuscript.
Comment 5: In Figures 5a–f, it is a little difficult to identify which regions (e.g., BFMO/Ni-Cr boundaries) are shown. Revising the figure captions for clarity would make the results easier to follow.
Response: We are grateful to the reviewer for this constructive suggestion.
Following the reviewer's suggestion, we have revised the figure captions of Figures 5a–f to make the identified regions clearer and the results easier to follow, reads as: ''Fig. 5 Polarization analysis of BFMO thin films. a,d Spontaneous polarization vectors (derived from B-site cation displacements) overlaid on HAADF-STEM images (Fig. S6) for a a randomly selected small grain on Ni-Cr marked as (a ) in Fig. 4a, and d a discontinuous-columnar grain on LNO/Ni-Cr marked as (c ) in Fig. 4c, where BFMO on LNO/Ni-Cr exhibits uniformity in both polarization vector alignment and angular distribution, confirming enhanced long-range polarization ordering compared to the disordered configuration on Ni-Cr, b,e corresponding atomic brightness contrast maps showing polarization amplitude, c,f corresponding atomic brightness contrast maps showing polarization angle. g P-E hysteresis loops of BFMO on Ni-Cr measured at 10 kHz (@RT). h,i P-E hysteresis loops of BFMO on Ni-Cr and LNO/Ni-Cr measured at 10 kHz before/after aging (@RT, 60, 120, and 180 °C), demonstrating superior aging resistance of the LNO-buffered sample.''.

General Comments: The authors have grown BFMO thin films on Ni-Cr substrates and have done some detailed analysis of defect engineering that explains the enhancement in ferroelectric properties. Overall response: We would like to express our gratitude for the valuable and constructive feedback provided by the reviewer, and emphasize that ''There are quite a lot of interesting results and analysis pertaining to the sample is carried out and which would definitely be interesting to the researchers working on defect engineering of multifunctional oxides.'' and ''Overall, it's a very interesting study and provides a different perspective and analysis. I accept this manuscript with major mandatory revision.''. In the following, we carefully address all comments from the reviewer.
Comment 1: The manuscripts never provide a justification on the choice of Mn and the specific atomic percentage (3 at.%) of Mn chosen to substitute in BFO.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the rationale behind the selection of Mn as the doping element and its concentration (3 at. %). We agree that clarifying this aspect is crucial for understanding our experimental design.
(1) The reason for the selection of Mn as the doping element
The selection of Mn is grounded in its established role as an effective dopant for mitigating the high leakage current in BFO, a necessity for measuring ferroelectric properties. This is based on two key mechanisms supported by literature [Ceram. Int. 41, S234-S239 (2015) and J. Alloy. Compd. 886, 161168 (2021)]1,2.
I. Charge compensation. Mn ions substitute on Fe-site, and their mixed valence states effectively compensate for the charge from oxygen vacancies, significantly reducing leakage current, an effect robustly demonstrated in prior works [Ceram. Int. 41, S234-S239 (2015)]1.
II. Structural stabilization. The strong Mn-O bond energy can enhance the stability of the perovskite structure [J. Alloy. Compd. 886, 161168 (2021)]2.
Consequently, Mn doping was chosen to solve the fundamental problem of high leakage in the sol-gel derived BFO thin films, enabling ferroelectric characterization.
(2) The reason for determining Mn doping concentration
Fig. R4 (Revised Supplementary Materials Fig. S12) Electrical performance measurements of BFMO thin films with Mn doping contents of 1, 3, and 5 mol. %, respectively. a,b Leakage current density versus applied electric field (I-E) curves of BFMO on rigid Pt/Ti/SiO /Si and flexible LNO/Ni-Cr, respectively, c,d P-E loops of BFMO on rigid Pt/Ti/SiO /Si and flexible LNO/Ni-Cr at 10 kHz, respectively.
The 3 mol. % (the same 3 at. %) Mn doping concentration was selected as the optimal compromise for sol-gel derived BiFeO thin films. This concentration effectively suppresses leakage current suppression to enable valid ferroelectric characterization, while minimizing the introduction of additional point defect that could interfere with polarization switching.
To identify the optimal doping level, we systematically prepared and compared BFO thin films with Mn concentrations of 1, 3, and 5 mol.%, respectively on both rigid (Pt/Ti/SiO /Si) and flexible (LNO/Ni-Cr) substrates. As shown in Figs. R4 a,b, at 3 mol. % Mn doping, the leakage current is reduced to a level that allows reliable ferroelectric testing, accompanied by significant modulation of coercive field (E ) and remanent polarization (P), resulting in significantly optimized ferroelectric properties (Figs. R4 c,d). This optimal performance at 3 mol. % is attributed to the balanced role of Mn ions. They suppress leakage by compensating for the oxygen vacancies, without introducing excessive additional point defects that would otherwise act as strong pinning centers that impede subsequent domain switching.
Following the reviewer's suggestion, Fig. R4 has been added into the revised Supplementary Materials as Fig. S12 considering the limited space availability. Additionally, we have added discussions, reads as: ''Preliminary experiments have determined that this optimal concentration can effectively suppress leakage current while significantly enhancing ferroelectric properties (Fig. S12).'' into the Part of ''Mn-doped BiFeO (BFMO) Thin Film Preparation'' in the Methods of the revised manuscript.
Comment 2: Most importantly, Mn is expected to increase the point defect densities, which in turn is expected to influence the electrical behavior. No mentioning on the role of Mn induced defects especially, considering the oxidation state changes that comes with Mn substitutions. A detailed analysis on octahedral distortions due to point defects can also be discussed and mentioned in the DFT studies.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment regarding the role of Mn-induced point defects. We agree that their impact on defect densities, oxidation states, and local structure is indeed important for understanding the electrical behavior.
In response, we have revisited our prior DFT calculations, performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) on Mn doped BFO with phase of R3c. These calculations utilized models constructed as a 1×2×3 supercell from the Materials Project database. Mn doping was introduced by substituting atoms at specific lattice sites. The electron exchange-correlation interactions were treated with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) and the projector augmented-wave (PAW) pseudopotential method. A plane-wave cutoff energy of 500 eV was used, and the self-consistent field calculations were converged until the energy change was below 10-5 eV.
Our analysis indicates that Mn doping introduces highly localized electronic states within the bandgap. As shown in Fig. R5, the overall band structure along the high-symmetry path Γ–X|Y–Γ–Z|R–Γ–T|U–Γ–V and fundamental bandgap remain largely unchanged upon Mn doping, suggesting that Mn predominantly acts as localized defect center, most consistently with a stable oxidation state (e.g., Mn3+). This strong localization of charge implies that the associated point defects and any charge fluctuations are confined to the immediate atomic environment. Consequently, while Mn doping increases point defect density, the electronic impact is localized, and this localization correspondingly suppresses long-range octahedral distortions in the average crystal structure.
Fig. R5 Band structures along the high-symmetry path Γ-X|Y-Γ-Z|R-Γ-T|U-Γ-V. a BFO, b BFMO.
We fully agree with the reviewer's insight regarding the necessity to precisely quantify local octahedral distortions induced by point defects. While the current DFT study successfully establishes the connection between electron localization and macroscopic structural stability, we acknowledge that a detailed quantitative analysis of the local atomic structure requires further investigation. Consequently, we have designated this as a key objective for our forthcoming research, planning to employ extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectroscopy to directly probe the Mn coordination environment.
Comment 3: The authors have written a statement ''Anisotropic strain field breaks the local symmetry and induce polarization gradients'' In principle yes, it’s a known phenomenon, however, the authors do not mention about the size of the polarization gradient and the strain gradients used in the calculations.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important aspect regarding the quantification of polarization gradient and strain gradient. We agree that specifying the magnitude of these parameters is essential for a comprehensive understanding of the calculated effects, and we appreciate the opportunity to clarify this point.

Comment 4: Most importantly, does the polarization gradient and strain gradient have the same directional features-not necessarily so. It would be nice if the authors can comment on the following:
a) What is the size of polarization gradient? And the size of strain gradient?
b) Do they have the same direction or what is the angular relation between them if the gradients are positioned in different directions?
c) Do they interact with each other?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for these insightful and critical questions regarding the directional relationship and interaction between polarization gradient and strain gradient. We have conducted further analysis based on phase-field simulations to address these specific points, as detailed below.
The phase-field simulations provide quantitative analysis of the polarization gradient and strain gradient induced by the dislocation cores, as shown in Fig. R6. The results indicate that the local polarization gradient is within the range of 108–109 C·m-3, while the corresponding strain gradient reaches a magnitude on the order of 108 m-1. Regarding the directional relationship, our analysis reveals that the polarization gradient and strain gradient do not exhibit a fixed angular correlation. Their spatial orientations are governed by distinct mechanisms: the strain gradient is primarily determined by the local lattice distortion around dislocations, whereas the polarization gradient follows the symmetry-breaking direction of the spontaneous polarization. Furthermore, within the framework of our model and the observation scale, no direct coupling interaction was found between these two gradient fields. Their evolutions appear to be driven by separate energetic contributions in the current system.

The strong correlation between free energy minimization and the emergence of ordered dislocation configurations provides compelling thermodynamic evidence for spontaneous self-assembly. These results confirm that the observed patterning corresponds to an energetically favored state, establishing strain engineering via parameter control as a pathway to guide defect organization in functional oxides, thereby clarifying the spontaneity of the defect arrangements.
While the phase-field simulations provide the distributions of both the polarization gradient and strain gradient, the direct calculation of the flexoelectric energy density is not feasible in the present study due to the lack of experimentally measured or reliably reported flexoelectric coefficients for this specific material system. In the future, our work will focus on quantitatively determining these coefficients and integrating them into our phase-field simulations, thereby enabling a complete thermodynamic description of electromechanical coupling in ferroelectric systems.
